issues.legal_issue: A prior judgment may operate as res judicata between co-plaintiffs when their conflicting interests were necessarily and actually decided.
material_facts: In an earlier suit, the present claimants and other parties appeared as co-plaintiffs seeking to protect their respective claimed shares in the same properties.
The defendant in that suit asserted that the properties belonged exclusively to the predecessor through whom one group of co-plaintiffs claimed title, thereby denying the other group’s title.
The court dismissed the suit after deciding that the properties belonged exclusively to that predecessor, and the dismissal was affirmed on appeal.
The later proceeding again concerned the parties’ competing claims of title to those properties.
issues.conclusion: The earlier judgment operated as res judicata on the question of title between the co-plaintiffs, so the parties whose title had failed could not agitate that same claim again.
issues.legal_principle: For res judicata between co-defendants, there must be an actual conflict of interest, deciding that conflict must have been necessary to grant the plaintiff relief, and the court must actually have decided the conflict; the same conditions apply, mutatis mutandis, between co-plaintiffs. A party bound by an earlier judgment must have had, or be deemed to have had, notice that the relevant issue was in dispute and would be decided. The doctrine is grounded in finality after genuine contest and should be applied according to substance rather than technical form. The Court applied Sheoparsan Singh v. Ramanandan Prasad Narayan Singh, referred to Chandu Lal v. Khalilur Rahaman, and cited Ram Bhaj v. Ahmad Saidakhtar Khan.

rule.if: co_plaintiff_title_dispute and (conflict_of_interest_between_co_plaintiffs and conflict_decision_necessary_for_relief and court_actually_decided_conflict and relevant_issue_notice)

predicates.co_plaintiff_title_dispute: The later proceeding concerns title claimed by parties who were co-plaintiffs in an earlier suit.
predicates.conflict_of_interest_between_co_plaintif: The co-plaintiffs asserted competing interests in the same subject matter.
predicates.conflict_decision_necessary_for_relief: Resolving the conflict between the co-plaintiffs was necessary to grant the relief sought in the earlier suit.
predicates.court_actually_decided_conflict: The earlier court expressly resolved the conflict between the co-plaintiffs.
predicates.relevant_issue_notice: The party to be bound had, or is treated as having had, notice that the relevant issue was in dispute and would be decided.

issues.definition: When co-plaintiffs later dispute title already contested with notice and necessarily and actually resolved in an earlier suit, the earlier judgment precludes relitigation of that title.

issues.legal_issue: An arbitration award contains an error of law apparent on its face when it rejects the binding effect of a prior judgment that operates as res judicata on the referred title dispute.
material_facts: A dispute over title was referred to an arbitrator in consolidation proceedings.
The first arbitrator held that certain claimants had no title, relying on an earlier judgment that determined the properties belonged exclusively to the predecessor of the opposing claimant.
A later arbitrator treated that judgment as only evidence and held that the claimants had title, without finding that they had acquired title by adverse possession.
The arbitration legislation applied to the arbitration proceedings under the consolidation law.
issues.conclusion: The later award was vitiated by an error of law apparent on its face and was liable to be set aside under section 30 of the Arbitration Act; the Court ultimately restored the first award.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 30 of the Arbitration Act, an award that sets forth an erroneous proposition of law may be set aside for an error of law apparent on its face. The Arbitration Act applies to proceedings before an arbitrator under the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, as held in Charan Singh v. Babulal. Because the earlier judgment operated as res judicata on title, an award stating that it did not operate as res judicata was legally erroneous.

predicates.arbitration_award_review: A court is reviewing an arbitration award made in a proceeding in which the arbitration law applies.
predicates.prior_judgment_bars_relitigation_of_refe: A prior judgment operates as res judicata on an issue referred to the arbitrator.
predicates.award_denies_prior_judgment_binding_effe: The award states or proceeds on the basis that the prior judgment does not bind the parties on that issue.

issues.definition: If an award under review denies the binding effect of a prior judgment that bars relitigation of the referred issue, the award is vitiated by an apparent error of law.

issues.legal_issue: A party may challenge in an appeal the correctness of an earlier order remitting an award when no appeal lay from that remittal order.
material_facts: An earlier order set aside an award and remitted the matter to the arbitrator for a fresh decision.
No appeal lay from that remittal order under section 39 of the Arbitration Act.
The correctness of that order was challenged in an appeal arising from the later decision in the arbitration proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The appellants were not precluded from challenging the correctness of the earlier remittal order in the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Section 39 of the Arbitration Act provides that no appeal lies from an order remitting an award under section 16. The Court held that, because the party could not appeal the remittal order when it was made, there was no reason to preclude a challenge to its correctness in the later appeal.

predicates.appeal_from_later_arbitration_decision: A party brings an appeal arising from a later decision in arbitration proceedings.
predicates.earlier_order_remitted_award: An earlier order set aside an award and sent the matter back to the arbitrator for a fresh decision.
predicates.no_appeal_lay_from_remittal_order: The governing appeal rules did not permit an appeal from the earlier remittal order.

issues.definition: When a party appeals from a later decision and could not appeal an earlier order remitting the award, the party may challenge the correctness of that earlier order in the later appeal.

issues.legal_issue: A court should restore a legally sound earlier award rather than remit the matter again when a further remittal would be an empty formality.
material_facts: The first award rested on the binding effect of an earlier judgment on the title dispute.
The later award rejected that binding effect and was vitiated by an error of law.
The Court considered that remitting the matter again to an arbitrator would be an empty formality.
issues.conclusion: The Court restored the first arbitrator’s award instead of remitting the matter again.
issues.legal_principle: Where, in the circumstances, another remittal would be an empty formality, the Court may grant effective relief by restoring the earlier award rather than sending the matter back again.

predicates.appeal_from_later_arbitration_decision: A party appeals from a later decision in arbitration proceedings.
predicates.earlier_award_legally_sound: An earlier award correctly resolved the referred dispute and is not vitiated by the identified legal error.
predicates.further_remittal_would_be_empty_formalit: Sending the matter back again would serve no useful purpose in the circumstances.

issues.definition: In an appeal from a later arbitration decision, when the earlier award is legally sound and another remittal would serve no useful purpose, the court restores the earlier award.
